so when i file the dispute... i'm not sure i need to mention the checkpoint timing, right? i mean, the breach is the breach. the data loss is 100% on them.

I wouldn’t leave the checkpoint timing out.

Even if the SIGKILL-without-SIGTERM point is the core of the 4.2 argument, checkpoint state is how anyone reading the dispute will decide *what actually got lost* and *who owns that loss*. Grace periods exist so you can drain and write a checkpoint. If you skip that in the filing, it looks like you’re asking them to treat uncheckpointed work as their problem by default. That’s usually not how these SLAs work, and it’s the first thing a facility will pull from the same logs.

A few distinctions that matter:

- A missing SIGTERM (if the log really shows that, and 4.2 really required one) is a *process* issue. It is not automatically “data loss is 100% on them.”
- Lost allocation and lost *results* are different claims. 9.1, if it exists as you described, is about credits/adjustments, not a guarantee that every unwritten checkpoint becomes their dollar figure.
- They will see last-checkpoint time anyway. If it was recent, include it — that *helps* you. If it was stale or missing, hiding it will get you a bounce, not $600.

I still don’t have the SLA or the daemon log in front of me, so I can’t tell you this is an objective breach or that a credit is guaranteed. Coincidence with a priority-queue pharma job also isn’t proof they “cleared the partition” for someone else, and I’d keep that theory out of the filing unless the contract actually forbids that preemption.

For NSF: don’t lead with “they stole the run.” Lead with what you can document: job id, 14:23:17 SIGKILL, no SIGTERM in the log you have, last successful checkpoint time, and that you’re requesting the 9.1 adjustment *and* a written incident note you can attach to the milestone. That’s explainable. A dispute that omits checkpointing is not.

If you paste 4.2, 9.1, and the log lines around 14:23:17 (plus last checkpoint), I’ll help you write an accurate dispute — not a cleaned-up one.
